opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to leverage. As a CEO you make thousands of decisions: who to hire, what feature to ship next, how to price things. Most of those are recoverable. If you make a mistake, you notice it and fix it within a few weeks. Choosing the track, meaning which market you're in and which problem you're solving, sits above all of that. It determines the ceiling of everything else.

If you pick the wrong track, a great team executing perfectly can still end up nowhere. The market might be too small, or the timing might be off, or the technology just isn't ready to create real value for users yet. Some markets are flooded with competitors and nobody makes money. If you pick the right track, the tide is with you. Even when you make a lot of execution mistakes, and every startup does, the market pulls you forward.

I learned this partly from my own experience. Coming from research and open source, my instinct was to focus on the technology itself: is this elegant, is this fast, is this technically impressive? But technical excellence doesn't automatically translate into a business. At some point you have to ask a harder question. Who desperately needs this, and is that need going to grow over the next five to ten years? For us, betting on generative AI for 3D content felt like that kind of track. Demand for 3D assets in games, film, e-commerce and XR is huge, and the traditional way of making them is extremely slow and expensive. That gap was the opportunity.

The other thing is that this decision can't be delegated. Engineers can optimize the code and the sales team can optimize the funnel, but nobody else in the company is positioned to step back and say we should be playing a different game entirely. That responsibility belongs to the CEO. So I try to spend a meaningful part of my time not on day-to-day execution but on making sure we're still running in the right direction. Running fast in the wrong direction is the most expensive mistake a startup can make.

r001.rationale: The response says the right market can pull a company forward despite execution mistakes, but it does not compare a lucky CEO on the right track with a hardworking CEO on an average track or suggest that people would prefer the former.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because I learned it the hard way. When we started Taichi, I was a researcher at heart. I thought if you build the best technology, the market will come to you. That's just not true. Technology is a multiplier, but the track you choose is the base number you're multiplying. If the base is small, it doesn't matter how brilliant your team is or how elegant your compiler is, you end up with a small result.

A CEO can be wrong about a lot of things and still recover. You can hire the wrong person and replace them. You can ship a bad feature and fix it next quarter. But if you're on the wrong track, every one of those good decisions is pushing in a direction that doesn't lead anywhere. You burn years, you burn the best people you've ever worked with, and at the end you realize the ceiling was set on day one.

What I mean by the right track is really three things. Is the problem big enough that a win matters? Is the timing right, meaning is there some shift, like a new hardware generation or a new user behavior, that makes now different from five years ago? And does our team have an unfair advantage here, not just interest? Lots of founders answer the third one and skip the first two. I did that. We built an incredibly fast language that people loved, but "people who want to write physics simulations in Python" is a passionate crowd, not a market that supports a venture-scale company.

And the uncomfortable part is that picking the track is the one job you can't delegate. Your engineers can't do it, your investors shouldn't do it, and your users will only tell you about the problem they have today. So the CEO's real job isn't managing the company. It's standing far enough back to see which mountain is worth climbing, before everyone else commits to the climb.

r001.rationale: The response says choosing the right track matters more than technology and other CEO decisions, but it does not compare a lucky CEO on the right track with a hardworking CEO on an average track or say which most people would prefer.

astra-6.text:
I think choosing the right business track is important because it determines how much your effort can actually accomplish. You can have a very strong team and execute very well, but if you’re solving a problem that customers don’t really care about, there’s a limit to what execution can fix.

For a CEO, the question is: Is this a real need? Is the timing right? And do we have some particular advantage in solving it? Those questions come before how fast we can build or how aggressively we can grow.

That doesn’t mean you can predict everything at the beginning. You have to talk to customers, test your assumptions, and adjust. But the CEO has to take responsibility for that direction, because everyone else’s time and effort depend on it.

r001.rationale: The response says choosing the right track matters more than execution can compensate for, but it does not suggest that most people would prefer a lucky CEO on the right track to a hardworking CEO on an average track.

sol-6.1.text:
I think choosing the right track determines whether all the work that follows can turn into something valuable. You can have a very strong team and execute well, but if you’re solving a problem people don’t really care about, that effort won’t get you very far.

For a CEO, the key questions are: Is there a real need? Is the timing right? And do we have some advantage that lets us solve it better? You’re making a commitment of the team’s time, often years of their lives. So you have to take that choice seriously.

That doesn’t mean you can predict everything at the beginning. You choose a direction, test your assumptions, listen to customers, and adjust. But you have to keep asking whether the opportunity itself is worth pursuing, rather than simply getting better at executing the original plan.

r001.rationale: The response says the right track matters more than strong execution on an unimportant problem, but it does not suggest that most people would prefer a lucky CEO over a hardworking CEO choosing an average track.
